title: Skill Sheet: Spinal Immobilization, Seated and Supine
body:
## Before you read the checklist

The national EMT psychomotor exam ended in 2023; skills are verified **in course** by your program using these same NREMT sheets, and states including NJ accept that verification. Both spinal stations live here because they share nearly every scored line and every critical criterion.

> **Key:** Seated (half-spine device, e.g. a KED) is `12 points`; supine (long backboard) is about `12–14 points` depending on the revision. Every line is `1 point`, no printed time limit. Modern practice has moved toward spinal *motion restriction* — collar and stretcher, backboard mainly for extrication — but the skill sheets still teach and score the classic sequence, and NJ protocols on backboard use vary, so follow your program.

## Station A — Seated patient, half-spine device (`12 points`)

Typical scenario: a stable patient still sitting in a car after a collision.

1. Takes or verbalizes appropriate PPE precautions — `1`
2. Directs assistant to place and maintain the head in a neutral, in-line position — `1`
3. Directs assistant to maintain manual stabilization of the head — `1`
4. Reassesses motor, sensory and circulatory function in each extremity — `1`
5. Applies an appropriately sized extrication collar — `1`
6. Positions the immobilization device behind the patient — `1`
7. Secures the device to the patient's torso — `1`
8. Evaluates torso fixation and adjusts as necessary — `1`
9. Evaluates and pads behind the patient's head as necessary — `1`
10. Secures the patient's head to the device — `1`
11. Verbalizes moving the patient to a long backboard or stretcher — `1`
12. Reassesses motor, sensory and circulatory function in each extremity — `1`

> **Trap:** Torso straps before head straps, always. Strapping the head first means every torso adjustment drags the cervical spine along with it, and it is scored out of order.

## Station B — Supine patient, long backboard (`12–14 points`)

Typical scenario: a patient found lying on the ground after a fall.

1. Takes or verbalizes appropriate PPE precautions — `1`
2. Directs assistant to place and maintain the head in a neutral, in-line position — `1`
3. Directs assistant to maintain manual stabilization of the head — `1`
4. Reassesses motor, sensory and circulatory function in each extremity — `1`
5. Applies an appropriately sized extrication collar — `1`
6. Positions the immobilization device appropriately (board alongside, or log-roll onto it) — `1`
7. Directs movement of the patient onto the device without compromising the integrity of the spine (coordinated log roll, you call the count) — `1`
8. Applies padding to voids between the torso and the board as necessary — `1`
9. Immobilizes the patient's torso to the device — `1`
10. Evaluates and pads behind the patient's head as necessary — `1`
11. Immobilizes the patient's head to the device — `1`
12. Secures the patient's legs to the device — `1`
13. Secures the patient's arms to the device — `1`
14. Reassesses motor, sensory and circulatory function in each extremity — `1`

## Numbers and rules worth having ready

| Thing | Rule |
|---|---|
| Head position | neutral, in line — stop if you meet resistance or pain increases |
| Manual stabilization | from first contact until the head is strapped to the device, never let go |
| Neuro checks | in all four extremities, before and after |
| Collar sizing | measured between the chin and the shoulder; a wrong-size collar is worse than none |
| Log roll | `3–4` people, the person holding the head calls the count |
| Padding | adult: behind the head as needed; child under about `8`: often behind the shoulders, because the head is relatively large |
| Pregnant patient on a board | tilt the whole board `15` degrees to the left |

## Critical criteria (automatic fail) — both stations

- Failure to take or verbalize appropriate PPE precautions
- Did not immediately direct or take manual stabilization of the head
- Did not properly apply an appropriately sized cervical collar before ordering the release of manual stabilization
- Released or ordered release of manual stabilization before it was maintained mechanically
- Manipulated or moved the patient excessively, causing potential spinal compromise
- Head immobilized to the device before the torso was sufficiently secured
- Device moves excessively up, down, left or right on the patient's torso
- Head immobilization allows for excessive movement
- Upon completion of immobilization, head is not in a neutral, in-line position
- Failure to reassess motor, sensory and circulatory function in each extremity after immobilizing the patient to the device
- Immobilized the patient to the board before the head was secured (supine station)
- Failure to manage the patient as a competent EMT
- Exhibits unacceptable affect with the patient or other personnel

## How to narrate it out loud

- **First words, every time:** "BSI on — partner, take manual in-line stabilization of the head and do not release until I tell you." Being slow to that line is an auto-fail.
- **Talk to the patient before touching.** "Don't move your head, even if it feels fine — let us do the moving."
- **Count the neuro exam limb by limb.** "Right hand: squeeze my fingers, feel that? Pulse present." Repeat for all four, before and after. Two scored lines.
- **Size the collar out loud.** "Measuring chin to shoulder — this is a regular. Collar on, but partner, keep holding — the collar alone is not enough."
- **Own the log roll.** "On my count, we roll together on three. One, two, three — roll." The head-holder calls it; if that is you, say so.
- **Check your own work before the head straps.** "Torso is snug, device isn't shifting, padding the void behind the head to keep it neutral — now securing the head."
- **Close the loop.** "Motor, sensory and circulation unchanged in all four extremities after immobilization."

> **On shift:** Real-world practice has shifted toward getting patients off rigid boards fast, because boards cause pressure injuries and breathing problems within about `30 minutes`. Know the sheet for the check-off, and know why the field is moving away from the board.
